Southern Caspian sprat (Clupeonella grimmi) exhibits a maximum body length that defines its growth potential within the Caspian Sea ecosystem. Field surveys conducted across multiple fishing grounds have established that the ultimate total length reaches 14.5 cm [Li = 14.5 cm], a value consistent with the moderate size typical of small pelagic clupeids inhabiting brackish environments. This asymptotic length is attained after several years of continuous somatic expansion, during which individuals transition from the planktonic larval stage through the juvenile phase and into the spawning adult condition. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, derived from length-weight regressions applied to representative samples, has been calculated at 22.67 grams [Wwi = 22.67 grams], reflecting the relatively slender body plan of this species compared to more deep-bodied congeners. Seasonal variation in body condition, driven by prey availability and reproductive investment, means that not all individuals achieve this maximum mass, but it remains a useful benchmark for comparative studies of life history strategies among Caspian clupeids. Growth trajectories suggest that the bulk of length increase occurs during the first two years post-hatching, after which annual increments diminish considerably as the fish approach their asymptotic size.

Reproductive development in Southern Caspian sprat is characterized by a well-defined size threshold at which gonad maturation commences. Examination of preserved material from multiple year classes indicates that the total length at puberty is 8.8 cm [Lp = 8.8 cm], a point at which roughly half of the individuals in a cohort exhibit developing gonads. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, estimated from the same length-weight relationship that governs adult body mass, is 5.04 grams [Wwp = 5.04 grams], representing roughly one-fifth of the ultimate somatic mass. This relatively early pubertal onset, occurring well before maximum length is reached, aligns with the pattern observed in many short-lived, iteroparous clupeids that begin reproducing at a modest fraction of their asymptotic size. The transition from immature juvenile to reproductively mature adult involves a pronounced acceleration of gametogenic activity, with vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males becoming histologically evident once this size threshold is crossed. Population-level variability around this pubertal size is modest, suggesting strong canalization of this life history transition under the relatively stable thermal regime of the southern Caspian basin.

Under the consistently warm thermal conditions prevalent in the southern Caspian Sea, where surface water temperatures routinely reach 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C] during the summer spawning season, embryonic development proceeds rapidly. Fertilized eggs, which are spherical, transparent, and approximately 0.8 millimeters in diameter, give rise to yolk-sac larvae after a brief incubation period of only 3 days [ab = 3 days] at a temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. The wet weight at birth, corresponding to the mass of the newly hatched prolarva immediately following chorion rupture, is approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams], a value reflecting the modest yolk reserves packaged into each egg. This tiny body mass places the newly emerged larva among the smallest of Caspian clupeids at the point of first exogenous feeding, imposing a narrow window for successful prey capture before endogenous reserves are exhausted. The rapid developmental rate at this elevated temperature (28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]) is presumably an adaptive response to the high metabolic demands of the warm, productive surface waters that characterize the species' primary nursery habitat. Larval mortality during this initial period is substantial, as is typical for small pelagic teleosts with low per-offspring investment.

Fecundity and spawning frequency in Southern Caspian sprat reflect a reproductive strategy adapted to the extended warm season of the southern Caspian. Females spawn throughout the year, though reproductive output peaks during spring and summer when surface temperatures are highest. The gonadosomatic index (GSI), which quantifies the proportion of body mass made up of ovarian tissue, reaches a maximum of 30% [GSI = 30%] under the thermal conditions of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. Across the broader population, mean GSI values are lower, with seasonal peaks averaging around 10% [GSI = 10%] during the breeding period.

Longevity in Southern Caspian sprat is constrained by both metabolic and ecological factors, resulting in a relatively short lifespan for a fish of its size. At the ambient temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], which is representative of the warm surface waters the species inhabits for much of the year, the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 2,920 days [am = approximately 2,920 days], or roughly eight years. This figure, derived from otolith-based age determination of the oldest individuals captured in research trawls, places the species at the shorter end of the longevity spectrum among Caspian clupeids, likely reflecting elevated metabolic costs associated with the warm thermal environment. Natural mortality in the wild is predominantly driven by predation from larger piscivores, including kilka-eating sturgeons and pelagic predators such as the Caspian seal, as well as by commercial fishing pressure, which targets adult aggregations during the spawning season. Post-reproductive senescence has not been systematically documented in this species, but the rapid decline in condition observed in the oldest age classes suggests that physiological deterioration accelerates after the fourth or fifth year, consistent with the life history syndrome of a fast-growing, early-maturing small pelagic fish.
